bullet_groups.bullet: Stored price levels in a std::map of std::list FIFOs with a hash map from order ID to list iterator for O(1) cancels, sustaining 1.26M events/sec over the full replay and a 1.2 µs per-update p99 on a separate 2M-event run

feedback.bullet: Stored price levels in a std::map of std::list FIFOs with a hash map from order ID to list iterator for O(1) cancels, sustaining 1.26M events/sec over the full replay and a 1.2 µs per-update p99 on a separate 2M-event run
feedback.problem: The project's headline throughput and tail-latency numbers (1.26M events/sec, 1.2 µs p99) are the last clause of the fourth bullet, behind a data-structure description. The 'µ' micro sign is a non-ASCII glyph that some ATS normalizers drop or mangle (e.g. '1.2 s' or '1.2 ?s'), which would turn a strong latency number into nonsense.
feedback.why_it_matters: For an HFT screen, throughput and p99 latency are the numbers the reader matches on. A recruiter skimming the project for 7 seconds sees correctness (bullet 1) but probably not speed, and a parser that drops the glyph corrupts the one latency figure on the page.
feedback.suggested_direction: Move this bullet up to second in the project so correctness and speed come first and the storage-engine comparison comes after. Write the unit as 'us' or 'microseconds' so it survives plain-text extraction. Optionally say 'price-time priority' for the std::list FIFOs, since that is the matching rule they implement and the term screeners match on.

feedback.bullet: Stored price levels in a std::map of std::list FIFOs with a hash map from order ID to list iterator for O(1) cancels, sustaining 1.26M events/sec over the full replay and a 1.2 µs per-update p99 on a separate 2M-event run
feedback.problem: The bullet leads with the data-structure choice and presents 'std::map of std::list' as the headline design, then attaches two numbers measured on two different runs ('over the full replay' vs 'on a separate 2M-event run'). A trading-systems reader sees node-based containers (std::map, std::list) as the textbook non-cache-friendly baseline and will wonder whether the candidate knows that, since nothing in the bullet signals it was a deliberate first version or a measured trade-off.
feedback.why_it_matters: In HFT screens the container choice is the first thing probed; stated without a reason it can read as 'did not consider cache locality' rather than 'chose simplicity and measured it', which undercuts the strongest project on the page. The two-run split also makes the reader stop to work out which number describes what.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: why std::map/std::list was chosen (baseline, correctness-first, or measured against an alternative); whether 1.26M events/sec and the 1.2 µs p99 come from the same build and machine setup (pinned/fixed clock as in bullet 3)
feedback.suggested_direction: Open with the result and the O(1)-cancel design idea (order ID -> iterator), then name the containers; if the node-based layout was a deliberate baseline, say so in a few words. Consider stating both numbers under one run description, or making clear the p99 run is the pinned/fixed-clock setup.

feedback.bullet: Stored price levels in a std::map of std::list FIFOs with a hash map from order ID to list iterator for O(1) cancels, sustaining 1.26M events/sec over the full replay and a 1.2 µs per-update p99 on a separate 2M-event run
feedback.problem: The first half ('std::map of std::list FIFOs with a hash map from order ID to list iterator') reads like a code declaration, not a sentence; the bold 1.26M events/sec headline is buried at the end. 'p99' and 'O(1)' are not recruiter vocabulary.
feedback.why_it_matters: The speed result is the most domain-relevant number on the page for HFT screeners, but I skipped this bullet during the skim because it opened with code types.
feedback.suggested_direction: Put the throughput result first and describe the data structure in words, keeping one distinctive term (hash map for instant cancels). E.g. 'Sustained 1.26M events/sec over the full replay (1.2 µs p99 per update) by keeping each price level as a FIFO queue in a sorted map, with a hash map from order ID so cancels take constant time.'

feedback.bullet: Stored price levels in a std::map of std::list FIFOs with a hash map from order ID to list iterator for O(1) cancels, sustaining 1.26M events/sec over the full replay and a 1.2 µs per-update p99 on a separate 2M-event run
feedback.problem: This is the core design decision of the whole project, but it comes last of four bullets, after the storage-backend bullet. Separately, 'std::map of std::list' is the first thing an HFT interviewer will push on, because both are node-based containers that allocate per node and chase pointers. The bullet also doesn't say what the 1.26M events/sec and 1.2 µs p99 time: book update alone, or parsing plus update.
feedback.why_it_matters: A trading-systems reader cares most about how the book is laid out. If they find it fourth, after a disk-storage comparison, the project reads as broader and less focused on the hot path than it is. If the timing scope isn't clear, the latency numbers lead to an awkward 'what exactly did you time?' follow-up.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the throughput and p99 timings include (book update only vs. feed decode + update)
feedback.suggested_direction: Move this bullet to second, right after the correctness bullet, so the order is correctness, then data structure and latency, then perf methodology, then storage. Add a few words on what was timed. Be ready to defend std::list against a contiguous or pooled alternative. Don't change the structure on the page.

feedback.bullet: Stored price levels in a std::map of std::list FIFOs with a hash map from order ID to list iterator for O(1) cancels, sustaining 1.26M events/sec over the full replay and a 1.2 µs per-update p99 on a separate 2M-event run
feedback.problem: Two problems. (1) 'on a separate 2M-event run' raises a flag: why isn't the p99 from the 50.9M replay? It reads like the latency number came from a friendlier run. (2) std::map plus std::list are node-based, cache-unfriendly containers that low-latency reviewers are trained to question. That's fine if it was a deliberate baseline, but the bullet presents it as the final design. It is also the most basic design bullet yet sits last, after the benchmarking bullets that depend on it.
feedback.why_it_matters: A trading-systems interviewer will probe the container choice and the measurement setup first. If the page suggests the numbers were picked selectively, the strongest project loses some trust.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the 1.2 µs covers (parsing + matching, or matching only) and why the p99 was measured on a separate run
feedback.suggested_direction: Move this bullet up to second so the reader sees the design before the benchmarks. Briefly say why latency was measured separately (e.g., timing instrumentation overhead), or drop 'separate' if it doesn't change the meaning.

feedback.bullet: Stored price levels in a std::map of std::list FIFOs with a hash map from order ID to list iterator for O(1) cancels, sustaining 1.26M events/sec over the full replay and a 1.2 µs per-update p99 on a separate 2M-event run
feedback.problem: The two performance numbers are well scoped by run, but the units and measurement boundary are not. The first bullet counts '50.9M real IEX exchange messages', while this one says 'events/sec' and 'per-update', so a reader can't tell whether messages, events and updates are the same unit. The bullet also doesn't say whether 1.26M/s and the 1.2 µs p99 were measured before or after the pinning and fixed-clock setup from bullet 3, or whether the p99 includes message parsing or only the book update. Only p99 is given, with no p50 to show the shape of the distribution.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the headline latency claim for an HFT screener, and the first follow-up question is 'what exactly is inside the timed region, and under what machine conditions?' A quick check gives 50.9M / 1.26M/s ≈ 40 s, which is only consistent if messages equal events. If they don't, the numbers look like they disagree.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether 'event' = 'IEX message' = 'update'; what the timed region covers (parse + book update vs. book update only); whether both runs used the pinned, fixed-clock setup; p50 next to p99 if it was measured
feedback.suggested_direction: Use one unit name across all four bullets and add a few words on the timed region and the setup. Consider moving the data-structure clause into its own short sentence so the numbers aren't buried after a 20-word design description, e.g. '...for O(1) cancels. On the pinned setup it sustained 1.26M messages/sec over the full replay and a 1.2 µs p99 book-update latency on a separate 2M-message run.'

bullet_groups.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the event log and benchmarked them on identical 2M-record workloads, where the B+ tree gave 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries at the cost of 27% more disk space

feedback.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the event log and benchmarked them on identical 2M-record workloads, where the B+ tree gave 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries at the cost of 27% more disk space
feedback.problem: 'the event log' never says what the log is for or why it needs range queries. An event log is usually append-heavy, so a reader expects the write side of the comparison and only gets reads and disk space.
feedback.why_it_matters: A trading-systems interviewer will ask straight away why reads and range queries matter for a matching engine's log. Without one clause of purpose, the bullet looks like a side benchmark rather than a design decision.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what reads or range queries the event log serves (e.g. replay by time window or order-ID lookup), and whether write throughput was measured
feedback.suggested_direction: Add a short purpose phrase after 'event log' that says what queries it answers. If write throughput was measured, add it so the trade-off reads in both directions. If not, leave the numbers as they are.

feedback.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the event log and benchmarked them on identical 2M-record workloads, where the B+ tree gave 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries at the cost of 27% more disk space
feedback.problem: 'the event log' appears without saying what the log is for in a matching engine (replay, audit, recovery, querying history), so the reader cannot judge why read throughput and range queries are the metrics that matter. The bullet also stops at the comparison and does not say which backend the engine uses or what the decision was.
feedback.why_it_matters: A hiring manager rewards design decisions, not benchmarks in isolation; without the purpose and the choice, the bullet reads as a side experiment rather than an engineering trade-off the candidate owned.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the event log stores and who reads it; which backend was kept and why; whether the workload was read-heavy (LSM trees are expected to win on writes, so the write side of the comparison is absent)
feedback.suggested_direction: Add a short purpose clause for the log before the tech names, and end with the decision rather than only the ratios, e.g. '...so I kept the B+ tree because replay is read-heavy' (only if true).

feedback.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the event log and benchmarked them on identical 2M-record workloads, where the B+ tree gave 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries at the cost of 27% more disk space
feedback.problem: The bullet stacks three comparison numbers (12.8x, 22x, 27%) but never says why the event log needed two storage backends or which one was chosen. 'B+ tree', 'LSM-tree' and 'range queries' are opaque to me, so I can only repeat 'he compared two things'.
feedback.why_it_matters: A recruiter cannot pass this on to a hiring manager as an accomplishment, and three ratios in one line read as metric stacking that I skim past.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the event log is used for (e.g. replay, lookups) and what decision came out of the benchmark
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the purpose of the event log and the decision, then the single most meaningful tradeoff number; consider dropping one of the three ratios. E.g. 'To decide how to store the engine's event log, built B+ tree and LSM-tree versions and benchmarked both on the same 2M records; the B+ tree read 12.8x faster for 27% more disk.'

feedback.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the event log and benchmarked them on identical 2M-record workloads, where the B+ tree gave 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries at the cost of 27% more disk space
feedback.problem: An event log is append-heavy, which is exactly the workload an LSM tree is built for. Yet the bullet reports only reads, range queries and disk space. It also doesn't say what the log is keyed on or what a 'range query' over it is (a time range? a sequence-number range? an order ID range?).
feedback.why_it_matters: Any storage-literate interviewer's first question will be 'and what about write throughput?' If write numbers are missing from a B+ tree vs. LSM comparison, the comparison looks cherry-picked even if it isn't. Without the key, '22x faster range queries' can't be judged.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the index is keyed on and what the range queries scan; whether write/ingest throughput was measured
feedback.suggested_direction: Name the key before the tech ('B+ tree and LSM-tree indexes on <key> for the event log'). If a write-side result exists, it belongs here more than disk space does. If it doesn't, keep the read framing but expect the write question.

feedback.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the event log and benchmarked them on identical 2M-record workloads, where the B+ tree gave 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries at the cost of 27% more disk space
feedback.problem: The comparison reports only the dimensions where the B+ tree wins (reads, range queries) and the disk-space cost, but omits write throughput, which is the reason anyone builds an LSM tree. A skeptical reader sees a one-sided benchmark. It also never says why an in-memory matching engine needs a persisted, range-queried 'event log', so the bullet reads like a separate database-course project bolted onto the order book.
feedback.why_it_matters: An HFT interviewer will immediately ask 'and writes?' and 'why is there a B+ tree anywhere near a matching engine?'. If the answers aren't obvious from the page, the bullet costs credibility instead of adding depth.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the event log is used for (replay? audit? recovery?) and how the two backends compared on writes
feedback.suggested_direction: Start with one short clause on what the event log is for, then give the trade-off from both sides. If the write result exists, state it next to the read result instead of only the disk cost.

feedback.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the event log and benchmarked them on identical 2M-record workloads, where the B+ tree gave 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries at the cost of 27% more disk space
feedback.problem: The comparison only reports read-side metrics, where B+ trees are expected to win, plus disk space. It leaves out write/append throughput, which is the reason anyone would pick an LSM tree and the main operation on an 'event log'. The bullet also doesn't say what the workload mix was ('identical 2M-record workloads' could be read-only or mixed) or which backend was kept.
feedback.why_it_matters: A storage-literate interviewer will read a read-only comparison of B+ tree vs. LSM as one-sided and ask whether writes were measured. As written, the bullet reads like a known textbook result rather than a tradeoff decision.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: read/write mix of the 2M-record workload; whether write throughput was measured; which backend the engine ended up using and why
feedback.suggested_direction: Name the workload mix in a couple of words. If a write-side result exists, give the tradeoff in both directions instead of reads plus disk only. If not, say the workload was read-heavy so the conclusion is scoped honestly.

bullet_groups.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries

feedback.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries
feedback.problem: The bullet opens with a 'Because' clause, so the verb comes 12 words in. It also stitches two techniques together ('precomputed... into a category tree' and 'with Redis caching') and ends on intent ('to cut database queries').
feedback.why_it_matters: Skimmers read the first few words of a bullet. Here those words are a constraint, not an action, so the caching and precomputation design is easy to miss.
feedback.suggested_direction: Start with the action ('Precomputed popular workflows into a category tree...'), then give the constraint as the reason ('...because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL table had strict access limits'). Keep the Redis clause last.

feedback.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries
feedback.problem: The 'Because...' opener puts 20+ words of constraint before the action, and the bullet ends on intent ('to cut database queries') with no observed effect. It also overlaps with the previous bullet's 65% result, so the reader cannot tell whether this change is part of that 65% or separate.
feedback.why_it_matters: Readers skim the first few words; starting with 'Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL' hides the verb, and an intent-only ending reads weaker than the bullets around it.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether this caching/category-tree change contributed to the 65% generation-time reduction in the previous bullet
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the verb ('Precomputed popular workflows into a category tree...') and move the access-limit constraint into a short trailing 'because' clause; if it is part of the 65%, consider merging the two bullets so one result covers both changes.

feedback.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries
feedback.problem: Opening with 'Because...' delays the action until mid-line, and 'Claude skill' is unexplained jargon for anyone outside AI tooling. 'To cut database queries' has no outcome attached, unlike the bullet above it.
feedback.why_it_matters: Slightly harder to skim than its sibling bullet; low impact since the first Capital One bullet already carries the result.
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the action ('Precomputed popular workflows into a category tree...') and move the access-limit reason into a short clause after it.

feedback.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries
feedback.problem: 'strict access limits' is ambiguous: rate limits, query quotas, permission restrictions, or latency? The design choice only makes sense if the reader knows which. The sentence also stacks three mechanisms: precomputation, a category tree, and a Redis cache.
feedback.why_it_matters: The 'because' framing is the right instinct, since it states the constraint behind the design. But the constraint is too blurry for the tradeoff to land, and an interviewer will spend the first question just finding out what the limit was.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what kind of access limit (rate/quota/permissions)
feedback.suggested_direction: Replace 'strict access limits' with the specific constraint. Keep 'category tree' as the distinctive noun. Consider whether the Redis clause carries its weight here, given that Redis caching appears again under TerpLabs.

feedback.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries
feedback.problem: 'Strict access limits' is vague: rate limits, permission restrictions, or query quotas each imply a different design. The bullet ends on intent ('to cut database queries') with no outcome. The 'Because ..., precomputed ...' opening drops the subject, which makes it read as a dangling clause.
feedback.why_it_matters: The constraint is the most interesting part of this bullet, and it's the part the reader can't decode. Without it, the design (category tree plus Redis cache) looks like generic caching.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what kind of access limit (rate, permissions, quota)
feedback.suggested_direction: Name the constraint concretely and put the subject first. If no measured outcome exists, consider merging this bullet into the previous one as the 'how', instead of keeping it as a standalone bullet with no result.

feedback.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries
feedback.problem: Starting with 'Because...' hides the action until the middle of the sentence. 'Strict access limits' is vague (rate limits? permissions? query quotas?), so the reason for the design isn't clear. 'To cut database queries' states an intent with no observed effect, and three mechanisms (precompute, category tree, Redis) are packed into one sentence.
feedback.why_it_matters: A skimmer reads the first words for the action and finds a dependent clause instead. A technical reader can't judge whether the caching design fits the constraint without knowing what the constraint was.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what kind of access limit (rate limit, read quota, permission scope)
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the verb and move the constraint after it, naming the constraint concretely, e.g. 'Precomputed popular workflows into a category tree the Claude skill searches first, and cached full workflows in Redis, because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL table had [specific limit].'

bullet_groups.bullet: Writing Java logic that sets the upper and lower bounds on EC2 capacity that Amazon Redshift reserves for operations like patching, balancing availability against cost, and backtesting it

feedback.bullet: Writing Java logic that sets the upper and lower bounds on EC2 capacity that Amazon Redshift reserves for operations like patching, balancing availability against cost, and backtesting it
feedback.problem: The trailing 'and backtesting it' attaches to the end of a long clause, so it reads as if the backtesting belongs to 'cost' or 'patching'. 'Backtesting' is a strong quant-screen keyword here, and it is buried in a dangling pronoun.
feedback.why_it_matters: Both LLM screeners and humans match 'backtesting' (it appears in the Jump C++ posting's scope). Here it is grammatically ambiguous and easy to skip, which wastes the one link between the AWS role and trading-style work.
feedback.suggested_direction: Reorder so the backtesting is its own verb phrase, e.g. 'Writing and backtesting Java logic that sets the upper and lower bounds on the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for operations like patching, balancing availability against cost'.

feedback.bullet: Writing Java logic that sets the upper and lower bounds on EC2 capacity that Amazon Redshift reserves for operations like patching, balancing availability against cost, and backtesting it
feedback.problem: The trailing 'and backtesting it' is grammatically detached (it reads as if 'availability against cost' is being backtested), and 'Writing Java logic' does not say whether the candidate owns the bounds algorithm, implements a spec, or builds the backtest harness.
feedback.why_it_matters: AWS is the top brand on the page; ambiguous ownership on its only bullet makes a hiring manager discount it to 'intern on a team' rather than 'owned a capacity-planning component'.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which part the candidate designs vs implements; what the backtest runs against (historical capacity/usage data)
feedback.suggested_direction: Split into a clear subject-verb structure: what the logic decides, how the candidate validates it via backtesting, and what part is theirs. Keep present tense since the role is ongoing.

feedback.bullet: Writing Java logic that sets the upper and lower bounds on EC2 capacity that Amazon Redshift reserves for operations like patching, balancing availability against cost, and backtesting it
feedback.problem: Three trailing clauses ('for operations like patching, balancing availability against cost, and backtesting it') chain together and 'it' at the end is ambiguous (the logic or the capacity?). The verb 'Writing' is weaker than describing what the logic decides.
feedback.why_it_matters: AWS is the top brand on the page and this is its only bullet; a reader has to reread to see that the backtesting applies to his own logic.
feedback.suggested_direction: Split the tradeoff from the validation: what the logic decides and why, then 'and am backtesting it against historical data' only if that is accurate; replace the dangling 'it' with the noun.

feedback.bullet: Writing Java logic that sets the upper and lower bounds on EC2 capacity that Amazon Redshift reserves for operations like patching, balancing availability against cost, and backtesting it
feedback.problem: The mechanism is missing. 'Java logic that sets the upper and lower bounds' doesn't say how the bounds are derived (rules, historical demand, a forecast). 'and backtesting it', tacked onto the end of a long sentence, reads like an afterthought.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the biggest brand on the page and the most quant-adjacent work in Experience (bounds, a cost/availability tradeoff, backtesting), but as written it describes a job duty rather than an engineering decision. The obvious interview question, 'how do you compute the bound?', has no anchor on the page.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what inputs or approach the bounds are computed from
feedback.suggested_direction: Name the method before the language, e.g. 'Writing Java logic that sets ... from <input/approach>'. Then make backtesting its own short clause ('and a backtest against <what>') rather than a trailing 'it'.

feedback.bullet: Writing Java logic that sets the upper and lower bounds on EC2 capacity that Amazon Redshift reserves for operations like patching, balancing availability against cost, and backtesting it
feedback.problem: The trailing ', and backtesting it' is stitched onto a phrase that already ends a thought, and 'it' could refer to the logic, the bounds, or the capacity. 'Writing Java logic' also blurs ownership: it doesn't say whether the candidate owns the bounding algorithm or is implementing a design someone else wrote.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the biggest brand on the page and its only bullet. A reader who has to re-parse it to work out what was built takes away less than the role deserves.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether the candidate designed the bounding approach or implemented it
feedback.suggested_direction: Split it into what the logic decides and how it's validated, with a clear subject for each, e.g. 'Writing the Java logic that decides how much EC2 capacity Redshift holds back for patching and other maintenance, and backtesting it against ...' Use only facts the candidate already has.

feedback.bullet: Writing Java logic that sets the upper and lower bounds on EC2 capacity that Amazon Redshift reserves for operations like patching, balancing availability against cost, and backtesting it
feedback.problem: The sentence trails off: ', and backtesting it' is attached to a participle phrase, so it reads as if 'balancing' and 'backtesting' are parallel. 'Writing Java logic' is also a weak verb phrase for what sounds like a capacity-planning policy.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the strongest brand on the page and it is mostly read for the brand. A clumsy sentence costs a re-read, and the backtesting part, the most quant-relevant word in it, gets lost at the end.
feedback.suggested_direction: Split the action and the validation so backtesting has a clear subject, e.g. 'Writing the Java policy that sets upper and lower bounds on the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for operations like patching, trading availability against cost, and backtesting it against historical usage' (only if the backtest is on historical usage; otherwise keep the existing scope).

bullet_groups.bullet: For a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR, built a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp’s candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D for a vision-language model, then tuned prompts so the model picks the right grasp more often

feedback.bullet: For a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR, built a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp’s candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D for a vision-language model, then tuned prompts so the model picks the right grasp more often
feedback.problem: 'picks the right grasp more often' is the only result, and it is unquantified. The bullet is the least relevant to systems/HFT but takes two full lines.
feedback.why_it_matters: For this target, the bullet costs two lines of reading and adds no systems or performance signal. The vague ending also invites a 'by how much?' question the page can't answer.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether a grasp-selection accuracy or success rate was measured
feedback.suggested_direction: If a measured rate exists, replace 'more often' with it. If not, shorten the bullet to fit one line (cut 'aimed at ICLR' or the Open3D detail) so the space goes to the systems content.

feedback.bullet: For a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR, built a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp's candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D for a vision-language model, then tuned prompts so the model picks the right grasp more often
feedback.problem: 'picks the right grasp more often' is an unmeasured outcome, and 'aimed at ICLR' signals a submission target rather than a result. The bullet has little to do with systems or latency work, yet takes two lines.
feedback.why_it_matters: For an HFT reader this line costs space without adding domain evidence, and the vague outcome invites 'how much more often?' with no answer on the page.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: how grasp-selection accuracy was judged, if any measurement exists
feedback.suggested_direction: Either state the measured improvement if one exists or shorten the bullet to one line focused on what was built, freeing space for the systems project.

feedback.bullet: For a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR, built a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp’s candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D for a vision-language model, then tuned prompts so the model picks the right grasp more often

feedback.why_it_matters: A latency-focused interviewer will ask 'from what to what?'. A percentage alone looks unanchored on a resume whose main project reports latency in microseconds.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: the before/after end-to-end latency in absolute terms, if known

bullet_groups.bullet: Traced an apparent 1.65x slowdown to the CPU frequency governor using perf counters and a null control book, then cut run-to-run variance from about 6% to 0.06% with core pinning and a fixed clock

feedback.bullet: Traced an apparent 1.65x slowdown to the CPU frequency governor using perf counters and a null control book, then cut run-to-run variance from about 6% to 0.06% with core pinning and a fixed clock
feedback.problem: 'an apparent 1.65x slowdown' does not say slowdown of what relative to what (between two builds? between runs?), and 'null control book' is unexplained jargon that a recruiter or ATS screener cannot restate.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the most HFT-relevant methodology bullet on the page (benchmark hygiene, isolating noise), but a non-specialist screener will skip it and a specialist must guess the setup before appreciating it.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the 1.65x was measured between; what the null control book is (e.g. a do-nothing book used to isolate harness cost)
feedback.suggested_direction: Name the comparison in 3-5 words after 'slowdown' and gloss 'null control book' with a short plain-English phrase; keep the 6% -> 0.06% result as is.

feedback.bullet: Traced an apparent 1.65x slowdown to the CPU frequency governor using perf counters and a null control book, then cut run-to-run variance from about 6% to 0.06% with core pinning and a fixed clock
feedback.problem: 'CPU frequency governor', 'null control book', 'core pinning' and 'run-to-run variance' are all jargon; a non-engineer cannot tell that this is about making benchmarks trustworthy rather than making the engine faster. 'Apparent' is doing a lot of work and is easy to miss.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is a strong debugging story for performance teams, but at screen I read '1.65x slowdown' and think the engine got slower; the point is lost before it reaches a hiring manager.
feedback.suggested_direction: Open with the goal in plain words (making benchmark results reliable) before the mechanism, and cut one of the two diagnostic tools if space is tight. E.g. 'Made benchmark results trustworthy: traced a false 1.65x slowdown to CPU power-scaling with perf counters, then pinned cores and fixed the clock to cut run-to-run variance from ~6% to 0.06%.'

feedback.bullet: Traced an apparent 1.65x slowdown to the CPU frequency governor using perf counters and a null control book, then cut run-to-run variance from about 6% to 0.06% with core pinning and a fixed clock
feedback.problem: 'null control book' is a term the candidate made up, and no reader can decode it (presumably a book that does no work, used to separate harness cost from book cost). '1.65x slowdown' has no reference point: slower than what, between which runs?
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the most HFT-relevant methodology bullet on the page, and the one invented noun slows down both the recruiter and the engineer. Neither can restate what the control was.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the null control book does, and what the 1.65x was measured against
feedback.suggested_direction: Swap 'null control book' for a plain description of its role, e.g. 'a no-op book as a control'. Anchor the 1.65x with a short 'between X and Y runs'.

feedback.bullet: Traced an apparent 1.65x slowdown to the CPU frequency governor using perf counters and a null control book, then cut run-to-run variance from about 6% to 0.06% with core pinning and a fixed clock
feedback.problem: This is the best evidence of benchmarking rigor on the page, but two phrases block it. 'Null control book' is unexplained: a reader can't tell whether it's a no-op book used to isolate harness cost. 'Run-to-run variance... 0.06%' doesn't say which metric (throughput? p99?), what statistic (CV? max-min spread?) or over how many runs. 0.06% is low enough that a performance engineer will want exactly that context before believing it.
feedback.why_it_matters: Unscoped variance figures are exactly what this reader checks. A 100x variance reduction with no metric or run count could be read as cherry-picked, which undercuts the bullet meant to prove the candidate measures carefully.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what 'null control book' is; which metric's variance and what statistic (e.g. coefficient of variation of throughput across N runs)
feedback.suggested_direction: Replace 'null control book' with a few plain words on its role (e.g. 'a no-op book as a control'), and name the metric and statistic behind 6% → 0.06%.

feedback.bullet: Built a C++17 order book and matching engine and replayed 50.9M real IEX exchange messages through it without ever resyncing to the exchange’s book, agreeing with the exchange on 99,122 of 99,123 fills and 100% of top-of-book prices

feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the fills were checked against

feedback.problem: 'Claude skill' and 'sub-skills' are vendor-specific terms that a trading-systems reader or recruiter won't know. 'guided by CloudWatch and OpenSearch latency logs', tacked onto the end, reads as tool name-dropping rather than part of the mechanism.

page_feedback.problem: Keyword gaps against the postings for terms the page already supports. I read 16 postings (IMC C++ Early Careers, IMC Quant Performance Engineer, Jump Campus C++ SWE, Akuna C++ SWE Intern, Point72 Quant SWE Intern, Virtu 2027 SWE Intern, DRW Quant Dev Intern, and others). Terms they repeat: C++ / modern C++ (C++17+), data structures and algorithms, Linux, performance profiling (perf, gprof, VTune), debugging (GDB, Valgrind, AddressSanitizer), low latency, market data, order entry / order lifecycle, backtesting, memory/caches, concurrency/multithreading, lock-free data structures, networking/protocol decoding, Python, Java, Git, CI, PostgreSQL. The resume already carries C++17, STL, POSIX, Linux perf, hardware counters, low-latency C++, data structures and algorithms, benchmarking, p99, backtesting, Python, Java, Git, CI/CD, PostgreSQL. It does not carry 'market data' (even though replaying 50.9M IEX exchange messages is market-data feed processing), 'Linux' as a standalone skill (only inside 'Linux perf'), 'CPU affinity' as a synonym for 'core pinning', or 'price-time priority' for the FIFO matching.

The rest of Experience is cloud and AI-tooling work (Java capacity logic, Claude skills, Kinesis/Lambda, VLM prompts, Redis). The project heading has no repository link, even though the header already links github.com/AmarDhillon05.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: An HFT reviewer will judge almost the whole candidacy on the order book. Being able to open the code is what turns '99,122 of 99,123 fills' from a claim into a verified result.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: If the repository is public, link it directly in the project heading line (e.g. replace or follow the tech list with the repo path). Keep the project above Experience as it is now, since that ordering is already right for this target.

page_feedback.problem: The IEX project has no link to code or a write-up, even though the header has a GitHub link.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: For a solo project carrying most of the domain weight, trading-firm reviewers want to verify it; the replay-accuracy and perf claims become far more credible with a repo one click away.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: If the repository is public, link it from the project title line.

page_feedback.problem: Plain-language load is uneven. The IEX bullets are rich in specialized nouns ('null control book', 'top-of-book', 'per-update p99'), and the experience bullets lean on platform jargon ('sub-skills', 'S3 staging hops', 'Prisma ORM'). A non-engineer screener can restate the IEX headline but would struggle with half the experience section.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: At HFT firms, recruiters with little technical background often do the first pass. If they can't restate a bullet, they skip it.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep the distinctive technical nouns, but put a plain verb phrase in front of each one that says what it does (e.g. what a 'null control book' was used for).

page_feedback.problem: Several Skills-section items have no supporting evidence anywhere on the page: Rust, Fargate, AWS CDK, Docker, GitHub Actions (CI/CD) and Pytest. Rust stands out in a C++/HFT context.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: LLM screeners increasingly cross-check skills against bullets, and HFT interviewers often pick an unsupported language from the skills list to probe. An unbacked 'Rust' can cost credibility in the interview.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep the items the candidate can defend in an interview, and cut or move to the end the ones that are only incidental. Keeping secondary tools in Skills is fine. Just make sure each one would survive one follow-up question.

page_feedback.problem: Tech that isn't load-bearing: 'POSIX' is in the project header but no bullet uses a POSIX mechanism (threads, mmap, sockets, affinity syscalls). Skills lists 'low-latency C++' as a self-applied label and 'data structures and algorithms' as filler. Rust, Fargate and AWS CDK appear nowhere in the bullets.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Systems interviewers routinely pick a Skills item at random and ask a probing question. Unsupported entries invite questions that the page can't back up, and 'low-latency C++' as a skill reads as a claim, not evidence.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Drop 'POSIX' from the project header unless a bullet shows it (core pinning could be described as the POSIX/affinity mechanism if that's what was used). Cut 'data structures and algorithms' and the 'low-latency C++' label, and let the project bullets show it. Keep only skills the candidate can defend.

page_feedback.problem: Skills lists 'low-latency C++' and 'top-down analysis' as skills, and lists Rust, C and Fargate, but none of these is shown in a bullet. 'Data structures and algorithms' is filler that every CS student could list.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: For an HFT reader, 'low-latency C++' as a self-applied label is a keyword claim; the IEX project already makes the case better. Unsupported entries invite questions the candidate may not want, such as 'walk me through a top-down analysis you did'.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Remove self-descriptive labels ('low-latency C++', 'data structures and algorithms'). Keep only tools the candidate can discuss in depth. Let the project bullets carry the latency claim.

page_feedback.problem: Parse-level details: (a) the certification line '(Nov 2024 – Nov 2027)' uses the same 'Mon YYYY – Mon YYYY' pattern as jobs, so Workday/Lever-style parsers can read it as an employment date range; (b) the non-ASCII glyphs 'µ' and curly apostrophes (’) appear in bullets; (c) the '(Client: Amazon Leo)' parenthetical sits in the company field and some parsers will store it as the employer name; (d) the project heading puts a pipe-separated tech list on the title line, which can merge into the parsed project title. Otherwise extraction is clean: reading order is correct, headings are standard (Education, Projects, Experience, Technical Skills), dates are consistent with en dashes, and contact info is on one parseable line.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: None of these blocks parsing, but each can put a slightly wrong value into a structured ATS field (a fake 3-year role, a garbled latency number, an employer named 'UMD App Development Contracting (Client: Amazon Leo)').
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Write the certification as 'issued Nov 2024, valid through Nov 2027' or just 'Nov 2024'. Use ASCII 'us' and straight apostrophes. Optionally move 'Client: Amazon Leo' into the title line or the bullet instead of the employer name.

page_feedback.problem: Roughly the bottom 15% of the page is blank, while the UMIACS and Capital One bullets are wrapped dense into two lines and the Experience section is visually compressed.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: This costs some polish only. The page is clean, single-column, consistently aligned and readable at 100% zoom.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Use the spare space for slightly more spacing between entries rather than more content, or leave it as is.

page_feedback.problem: Roughly the bottom 15% of the page is empty while several bullets are compressed into dense two-line sentences.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Minor visual imbalance; the space could give the project bullets breathing room or a short clarifying clause.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Use the space for clarifications flagged in bullet feedback rather than new bullets or more metrics.

page_feedback.problem: Rust and C appear in Languages with no supporting work on the page.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Trading-firm interviewers often pick a listed language to probe; an unsupported listing is a small credibility risk.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep only languages the candidate is comfortable being interviewed in.

page_feedback.problem: The Projects section sits above Experience, so the AWS and Capital One brands appear in the lower half of the page.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: For this domain the C++ project is the right lead, so this is a reasonable choice; the cost is that the brands take a beat longer to find in a 7-second skim.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep the order for this target; no change needed unless the same page is reused for general SWE.

page_feedback.problem: Bottom of the page has noticeable unused whitespace while several bullets are dense two-liners.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Minor visual imbalance; the space could relieve density in the project section.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Use the room to loosen the project bullets (e.g. splitting the purpose from the metric) rather than adding content.

page_feedback.problem: Nearly every bullet runs the full two lines, and the project section is four dense two-line bullets in a row, while roughly the bottom 15% of the page is empty.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The densest, most important section is the hardest to skim. Meanwhile, unused space suggests the cramming wasn't forced by length.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Use the clarifications above to replace words, not add them. Slightly increase spacing between project bullets or sections so the project block breathes.

page_feedback.problem: About 15% of the page at the bottom is empty, while the AWS role (the strongest brand) has a single bullet and the UMIACS bullet takes two lines for low-domain-value content.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The space budget doesn't match what this reader cares about. Systems evidence is thin outside the one project.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: No new facts are needed. Use the space to make the AWS bullet clearer (split the what and the how) rather than adding content elsewhere.

page_feedback.problem: The IEX project (Jul–Aug 2026) runs concurrently with the full-time Capital One internship (Jun–Aug 2026).
page_feedback.why_it_matters: An interviewer may ask how a 50.9M-message replay system with careful benchmarking was built in the evenings of a full-time internship. This is plausible, but the candidate should be ready for it.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: No change to the page is needed. Be ready to explain the timeline and scope in an interview.

page_feedback.problem: About 15% of the page at the bottom is empty, while several bullets are dense two-liners packing design, numbers and setup into one sentence.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The order-book bullets are the strongest content but the hardest to read quickly. The unused space could let them breathe.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Use the free vertical space for slightly more spacing between bullets or sections, or split the densest project bullet into design and result, without adding new content.

page_feedback.problem: Within the project bullets, bold falls on 50.9M, 12.8x and 1.26M events/sec, but not on the 99,122 of 99,123 correctness result or the 1.2 µs p99.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: For this audience, exact-match correctness and tail latency are the headline signals. Bolding message volume and throughput instead points the skimmer at the less distinctive numbers.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Move bold anchors to the correctness match and the p99, keeping one per bullet.
